title: Test bench: which model to use and what it'll cost you
pitch: A program that sends the same job to three models, saves all three answers, and logs how many tokens each one used and what it costs. At the end it spits out a table you use to decide, figures in hand, which one suits that specific task.
outcome: A folder with working code and a tabla.md file you can show a boss or a client: same prompt, three answers, tokens, seconds, cost per call, cost per thousand calls, and your quality score. With the decision written out at the end, and why.
time: 3-4 hours the first time, counting signing up with the providers
requires: Python 3.10 or higher installed. Check by typing 'python --version' in the terminal
A text editor for creating files. VS Code works and is free
At least one API key. Google AI Studio gives one free, with requests-per-minute limits and no card required; OpenAI requires loading balance up front, minimum $5, and has no free plan for the API
With two keys (OpenAI and Google) you get the three-model comparison built here. With just one it still works: you compare two models from the same provider
Knowing what a token is and why you pay for them. That's covered in this area
Getting around the terminal with 'cd' and 'mkdir'

structure.what: Where your API keys live. This file never gets pushed anywhere or emailed
The list of models to compare and what each million tokens costs. Edited by hand when prices change
The job. Just one, the same for everyone: change the prompt halfway through and the comparison is worthless
Talks to the three APIs. Each one asks for things differently and this hides that behind a single function
Asks each provider what models it has available today. Run before spending, so you don't fail on a stale name
The main program: sends the prompt to everyone, times it, calculates the cost, and saves it all to a dated file
Reads what was saved, lets you score the answers, and prints the decision table on screen and in markdown
One comparison per file, with the date in the name. This is your history: three months from now you'll see how prices and quality changed

steps.title: Set up the folder and isolate the project
steps.why: A virtual environment is a copy of Python that lives inside your folder. What you install there doesn't clutter the rest of your computer, and if something breaks you delete the folder and that's it. It's the first thing you do in any Python project, always.
steps.code:
# 1. Check you have Python. It has to say 3.10 or higher.
python --version

# 2. Create the project folder and go into it
mkdir comparador
cd comparador
mkdir resultados

# 3. Virtual environment: a copy of Python just for this project, so
#    what you install here doesn't touch the rest of your computer
python -m venv .venv

# 4. Activate it. Mac and Linux:
source .venv/bin/activate
# Windows PowerShell:   .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
# Windows CMD:          .venv\Scripts\activate.bat

# 5. The only library you need. requests is the one that makes internet calls.
pip install requests
steps.expected: 'python --version' says 3.10 or higher. After activating, your terminal line starts with (.venv). And pip finishes with 'Successfully installed requests-2.32.x'.
steps.trouble: On Windows, typing 'python' sometimes opens the Microsoft Store: use 'py -3' instead, or install Python from python.org checking the 'Add python.exe to PATH' box. If PowerShell says script execution is disabled when activating the environment, the fastest fix is to open CMD and use '.venv\Scripts\activate.bat' instead of fighting the permissions.

steps.title: Keep the keys out of the code
steps.why: An API key is the password that identifies you to the provider and against which you get billed. Write it inside a .py file and it ends up in every copy, screenshot, or repository you share. That's why it goes in a separate file, .env, that the code reads at startup and that never gets shared. Serious warning: if a key leaks to GitHub or a chat, consider it burned. Go to the provider's dashboard, delete it, and create a new one. That deletion is irreversible, and that's exactly what you want.
steps.code:
cd comparador

# .env is the file where the keys live. Never gets pushed anywhere, ever.
cat > .env <<'EOF'
OPENAI_API_KEY=paste-your-key-here
GOOGLE_API_KEY=paste-your-key-here
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=
EOF

# .gitignore tells Git these files don't leave your computer
cat > .gitignore <<'EOF'
.env
.venv/
__pycache__/
EOF

# On Windows with PowerShell this "cat > file <<EOF" doesn't exist. Create
# both files from your editor and paste the content between EOF and EOF.
# Watch out: the name starts with a dot, .env, and has no extension.

# Now open .env and replace "paste-your-key-here" with your real keys.
cat .env
steps.expected: 'cat .env' shows you three lines, two of them with your real keys pasted in. OpenAI's starts with 'sk-'. Anthropic's can stay empty: the program skips models whose key is missing.
steps.trouble: The typical mistake is spaces and quotes: it's written OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-abc123, no spaces around the equals sign and no quotes. If a line break sneaks in while pasting the key from the browser, delete it. About money: OpenAI requires you to load balance up front, minimum $5, and the whole project will use less than $0.10. Google AI Studio gives a free key, with requests-per-minute limits and no card required.

steps.title: Write the list of models and their prices
steps.why: Prices don't go in the code because they change. They go in a data file you update in thirty seconds without touching a line of program. The record is always the same: who serves it, what the model is called, what the million input tokens cost, and what the million output tokens cost. Notice the difference: output costs 4 to 5 times more than input. That's why a long answer costs you a lot more than a long prompt.
steps.expected: A file called modelos.json inside comparador/, with four models in it. If you open it in the editor and don't see any line underlined in red, the JSON is written correctly.
steps.trouble: The classic JSON mistake is a trailing comma before a closing bracket or brace: JSON doesn't forgive it. If the editor underlines something, that's it 90% of the time. And prices use a decimal point (0.40), never a comma (0,40).

steps.title: Write the job all three will receive
steps.why: Here's the trap in almost every comparison floating around out there: they compare models with different prompts, or with a toy job like 'write a poem'. That doesn't decide anything. The prompt has to be your real work, with constraints you can check one by one: how many words, what tone, what it says and doesn't say. That way you score it later without arguing with yourself.
steps.code:
cd comparador

cat > prompt.txt <<'EOF'
You are the customer support team for Muebles Verdi, a Spanish online furniture store.

A customer writes to return a €189 desk chair they bought 22 days ago. They say it
hurts their back. The chair is used but not broken. Our policy accepts returns up
to 30 days if the product is complete with its original box.

Write the reply to the customer meeting these requirements:
- Maximum 150 words.
- Warm, informal tone, no call-center phrasing.
- Accept the return and explain the two steps: request free pickup from their
  account and put the chair back in its original box.
- Don't promise a refund date: just say it happens within 5 business days from
  when the chair reaches the warehouse.
- End with a question that invites a reply.
EOF

# On Windows: create prompt.txt from the editor and paste the text above,
# what's between EOF and EOF, without the EOF lines.
cat prompt.txt
steps.expected: 'cat prompt.txt' gives you back the whole job, about 15 lines. Notice that each constraint can be checked with your eyes: counting words, checking whether it promises a date, checking whether it ends in a question.
steps.trouble: If you get 'command not found: cat' you're in PowerShell and not a Unix-style terminal: create the file from VS Code and paste the text, it's exactly the same. And check it's called prompt.txt and not prompt.txt.txt, which is what Windows Notepad does without warning you.

steps.title: Write the translator that talks to the three APIs
steps.why: The three APIs do the same thing but differently: OpenAI wants the key in an 'Authorization' header, Anthropic in 'x-api-key', Google in 'x-goog-api-key'. And each one counts tokens its own way. This file hides those differences behind a single function, llamar(), which always returns the same thing: text, input tokens, and output tokens. Notice one detail that costs real money: Gemini bills the tokens it spends thinking as output, and they arrive in a separate field you have to add in by hand.
steps.expected: Save the file as comparador/proveedores.py. To check for typos, run 'python -c "import proveedores"' from the comparador folder: if it says absolutely nothing, it's fine.
steps.trouble: If importing it says 'ModuleNotFoundError: No module named requests', either the virtual environment isn't active or you're missing the 'pip install requests' from step one. Quick check: does your terminal line start with (.venv)?

steps.title: Ask which models exist today, before you pay
steps.why: Model names go stale. A 'gpt-4.1-mini' from today can be a 404 error six months from now, and what the API returns isn't always understandable at a glance. This asks the provider itself for its list and marks which of yours still exist. It's free: asking for the model list doesn't spend tokens.
steps.code:
"""Checks that the identifiers in modelos.json really exist today.

Model names go stale. This runs before spending a cent: if an identifier
no longer shows up, you fix it and avoid the error.
"""

import json
from pathlib import Path

import proveedores

CARPETA = Path(__file__).parent

proveedores.cargar_env()
config = json.loads((CARPETA / "modelos.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
pedidos = config["modelos"]

# One block per provider, no repeats: hence the set with braces
for proveedor in sorted({m["proveedor"] for m in pedidos}):
    if not proveedores.clave_de(proveedor):
        print(f"\n[{proveedor}] no key in .env: skipping")
        continue
    try:
        disponibles = proveedores.listar(proveedor)
    except Exception as error:
        print(f"\n[{proveedor}] couldn't get the list: {error}")
        continue

    print(f"\n[{proveedor}] {len(disponibles)} models available.")
    print("  The ones you have set in modelos.json:")
    for m in pedidos:
        if m["proveedor"] != proveedor:
            continue
        marca = "EXISTS     " if m["modelo"] in disponibles else "MISSING    "
        print(f"    {marca}{m['modelo']}")
    print("  First from the full list:")
    for nombre in disponibles[:12]:
        print(f"    - {nombre}")
steps.expected: Running 'python listar_modelos.py' shows a block per provider, with the word EXISTS next to each of your models and a sample of what's available. Providers with no key show as skipped.
steps.trouble: If a model shows as MISSING, copy the closest matching identifier from the list below and change it in modelos.json. If the response is a 401 error, the key is pasted wrong. If it's a 403 on OpenAI, it's almost always that the account has no balance loaded.

steps.title: Send the same prompt to everyone and save what happens
steps.why: This is the heart of the project. It goes through the model list, skips the ones with no key, times each call, reads the tokens the API itself returns (doesn't estimate them: reads them), and calculates the cost with your file's prices. It saves everything with a date, full response included. Saving matters: every call costs money and you don't want to pay for it again just to look at the table once more.
steps.code:
"""Sends the same prompt to every model and logs what each one costs."""

import json
import time
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import proveedores

CARPETA = Path(__file__).parent
RESULTADOS = CARPETA / "resultados"


def coste_en_dolares(entrada, salida, modelo):
    """Input and output tokens have different rates."""
    return (
        entrada / 1_000_000 * modelo["precio_entrada_por_millon"]
        + salida / 1_000_000 * modelo["precio_salida_por_millon"]
    )


def main():
    proveedores.cargar_env()
    RESULTADOS.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

    prompt = (CARPETA / "prompt.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip()
    config = json.loads((CARPETA / "modelos.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

    print(f"Prompt: {len(prompt)} characters")
    print(f"Models in the list: {len(config['modelos'])}\n")

    resultados = []
    for modelo in config["modelos"]:
        alias = modelo["alias"]

        # No key, no call: warn and move to the next one
        if not proveedores.clave_de(modelo["proveedor"]):
            print(f"[skipped] {alias}: no {modelo['proveedor']} key in .env")
            continue

        print(f"[calling] {alias} ...", flush=True)
        empezo = time.time()
        try:
            respuesta = proveedores.llamar(
                modelo["proveedor"], modelo["modelo"], prompt
            )
        except Exception as error:
            # One failing can't take down the whole comparison
            print(f"[failed] {alias}: {error}\n")
            continue
        segundos = round(time.time() - empezo, 1)

        coste = coste_en_dolares(
            respuesta["tokens_entrada"], respuesta["tokens_salida"], modelo
        )
        resultados.append({
            "alias": alias,
            "proveedor": modelo["proveedor"],
            "modelo": modelo["modelo"],
            "tokens_entrada": respuesta["tokens_entrada"],
            "tokens_salida": respuesta["tokens_salida"],
            "segundos": segundos,
            "coste_usd": round(coste, 6),
            "texto": respuesta["texto"],
            "nota": None,  # you set this later, in tabla.py
        })
        print(
            f"           {respuesta['tokens_entrada']} input tokens, "
            f"{respuesta['tokens_salida']} output, {segundos} s, "
            f"{coste:.6f} $\n"
        )

    if not resultados:
        print("No model answered. Check .env and try again.")
        return

    # One file per comparison, with the date in the name: that's the history
    nombre = datetime.now().strftime("comparacion_%Y-%m-%d_%H%M%S.json")
    (RESULTADOS / nombre).write_text(
        json.dumps({
            "fecha": datetime.now().isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
            "prompt": prompt,
            "nota_precios": config.get("nota_precios", ""),
            "resultados": resultados,
        }, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2),
        encoding="utf-8",
    )

    total = sum(r["coste_usd"] for r in resultados)
    print(f"{len(resultados)} answers saved to resultados/{nombre}")
    print(f"This comparison cost you {total:.6f} $")
    print("Now run: python tabla.py")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
steps.expected: Save this as comparador/comparar.py and run it with 'python comparar.py'. You'll see one [calling] line per model, and below it its tokens, its seconds, and its cost with six decimals, something like 0.000772 $. It finishes saying how many answers it saved and the total spend, which will be under $0.01.
steps.trouble: If a model returns 'Unsupported parameter: max_tokens', that model is one of the newer ones that wants the field named 'max_completion_tokens': change the name inside the _openai function. If you get a 429, you went too fast for Google's free tier: wait a minute and try again.

steps.title: Score the answers and get the decision table
steps.why: The machine counts tokens and cost. It doesn't judge quality: that's you, reading. This file shows you each answer, asks you for a score from 1 to 5, and saves it inside the same results file. Then it sorts by cost and adds the column that really decides: what a thousand calls would cost. A $0.003 difference tells nobody anything; $3.20 a month versus $0.60 does.
steps.code:
"""Reads the latest comparison, lets you score it, and produces the decision table."""

import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

CARPETA = Path(__file__).parent
RESULTADOS = CARPETA / "resultados"

EJECUCIONES = 1000  # the cost of one call says nothing; a thousand does


def ultimo_archivo():
    archivos = sorted(RESULTADOS.glob("comparacion_*.json"))
    if not archivos:
        print("No comparisons yet. Run first: python comparar.py")
        sys.exit(1)
    return archivos[-1]


def pedir_notas(datos, archivo):
    """The machine counts tokens. You judge quality."""
    pendientes = [r for r in datos["resultados"] if r.get("nota") is None]
    if not pendientes:
        return
    print("Read each answer and score it from 1 to 5 (Enter to skip).\n")
    for resultado in pendientes:
        print("=" * 70)
        print(f"{resultado['alias']}  ({resultado['modelo']})")
        print("=" * 70)
        print(resultado["texto"].strip()[:1200])
        print()
        while True:
            nota = input("Score 1 to 5: ").strip()
            if nota == "":
                break
            if nota in {"1", "2", "3", "4", "5"}:
                resultado["nota"] = int(nota)
                break
            print("Type a number from 1 to 5, or Enter to skip.")
        print()
    # The scores get saved into the same file: no need to pay again
    archivo.write_text(
        json.dumps(datos, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2), encoding="utf-8"
    )


def fila(r):
    nota = r["nota"] if r["nota"] else "-"
    return (
        f"{r['alias'][:17]:<18}{r['proveedor']:<11}"
        f"{r['tokens_entrada']:>7}{r['tokens_salida']:>8}{r['segundos']:>6}"
        f"{r['coste_usd']:>10.6f}{r['coste_usd'] * EJECUCIONES:>9.2f}"
        f"{nota:>6}"
    )


def recomendacion(resultados):
    """The cheapest among the best-scored. No mystery."""
    puntuados = [r for r in resultados if r.get("nota")]
    if len(puntuados) < 2:
        return "Score at least two answers to get a recommendation."
    mejor = max(r["nota"] for r in puntuados)
    candidatos = [r for r in puntuados if r["nota"] == mejor]
    elegido = min(candidatos, key=lambda r: r["coste_usd"])
    caro = max(puntuados, key=lambda r: r["coste_usd"])
    if caro["alias"] == elegido["alias"]:
        return (
            f"Use {elegido['alias']}: it's the one you scored highest and also "
            "the most expensive, so here you're actually paying for real quality."
        )
    veces = caro["coste_usd"] / elegido["coste_usd"] if elegido["coste_usd"] else 0
    return (
        f"Use {elegido['alias']}: score {mejor}/5 and {veces:.1f} times cheaper "
        f"than {caro['alias']}."
    )


def main():
    archivo = Path(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else ultimo_archivo()
    datos = json.loads(archivo.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    pedir_notas(datos, archivo)

    resultados = sorted(datos["resultados"], key=lambda r: r["coste_usd"])
    cabecera = (
        f"{'MODEL':<18}{'PROVIDER':<11}{'TOK-IN':>7}{'TOK-OUT':>8}"
        f"{'SEC':>6}{'COST $':>10}{'x1000 $':>9}{'SCORE':>6}"
    )
    lineas = [cabecera, "-" * len(cabecera)] + [fila(r) for r in resultados]

    print()
    print(f"File: {archivo.name}")
    print("\n".join(lineas))
    print()
    print(recomendacion(resultados))

    # The same table in markdown, to show whoever isn't looking at your terminal
    md = [
        "# Model comparison", "",
        f"Date: {datos['fecha']}", "",
        "## Prompt", "", "```", datos["prompt"], "```", "",
        "## Table", "",
        "| Model | Provider | Input tokens | Output tokens | Seconds "
        "| Cost $ | 1000 calls $ | Score |",
        "| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |",
    ]
    for r in resultados:
        md.append(
            f"| {r['alias']} | {r['proveedor']} | {r['tokens_entrada']} "
            f"| {r['tokens_salida']} | {r['segundos']} | {r['coste_usd']:.6f} "
            f"| {r['coste_usd'] * EJECUCIONES:.2f} | {r['nota'] or '-'} |"
        )
    md += [
        "", f"**Decision:** {recomendacion(resultados)}", "",
        f"_{datos.get('nota_precios', '')}_", "",
        "## Full answers", "",
    ]
    for r in resultados:
        md += [f"### {r['alias']} ({r['modelo']})", "", r["texto"].strip(), ""]

    (RESULTADOS / "tabla.md").write_text("\n".join(md), encoding="utf-8")
    print("Markdown table: resultados/tabla.md")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
steps.expected: Save this as comparador/tabla.py and run 'python tabla.py'. It'll show you the answers one by one for you to score, and at the end prints the aligned table, a recommendation sentence, and the resultados/tabla.md file. Run it a second time and it won't ask again: the scores stayed saved.
steps.trouble: If you get 'No comparisons yet', comparar.py didn't manage to save anything: go back to the previous step and check what error it gave. If you want to score from scratch again, delete the results file and run comparar.py again, knowing that costs money again.

steps.title: Change the task and check the decision changes
steps.why: Here's the lesson of the whole project. With the writing task, the expensive model probably wins, and by a little. With a data-extraction-to-JSON task, where there's only one correct answer, it's normal for the cheap one to score just as well and cost ten times less. There's no such thing as 'the best model': there's the best model for this task, and now you have the tool to prove it with numbers instead of opinions.
steps.code:
cd comparador
source .venv/bin/activate     # Windows CMD: .venv\Scripts\activate.bat

# Save the table you already have under another name, so you don't overwrite it
cp resultados/tabla.md resultados/tabla_redaccion.md

# Now a completely different job: extracting data, not writing
cat > prompt.txt <<'EOF'
From the email below, extract the data as JSON with these exact keys:
cliente, pedido, importe_eur, motivo, urgente (true or false).
Write nothing but the JSON, no explanations and no code block.

EMAIL:
Hi, I'm Marta Ruiz. Order MV-40871 arrived yesterday with the back leg broken.
I paid €189.90 and I need it by Monday because I'm moving. Best regards.
EOF

# Same comparator, different job. Run it again and score again.
python comparar.py
python tabla.py
steps.expected: A second table with the same structure and different scores. In the JSON extraction, scores bunch together, because almost everyone gets it right, and the recommendation shifts to the cheap model. You end up with two files: tabla_redaccion.md and tabla.md.
steps.trouble: If some model returns the JSON wrapped in a code block despite the prompt forbidding it, that's not your mistake: it's a real difference between models and it's exactly what you're measuring. Lower its score and note it, because in production that means extra lines of code to clean up the answer.

checks: You run comparar.py and at least two different models answer, and a new file shows up in resultados/ with the date and time in the name
You search for 'sk-' across every file in the project and it only shows up inside .env: not in the .py files, not in modelos.json, not in the results
You empty out a key from .env, run it again, and that model shows as skipped while the others keep going. The program doesn't crash
The tokens in the table come from each API's own response, not a count you did separately, and you can point to the exact line of code where they're read
You show resultados/tabla.md to someone who hasn't seen the code and in under a minute they understand which model you'd pick and why
You change the prompt, run it again, and can say out loud what a thousand runs would cost with each model and which one you'd pick this time
extend: Send the same prompt three times in a row to the same model and save all three. You'll see neither the answers nor the token counts are identical: that's variability, and from there the average is worth more than a single try

Swap the single prompt for a file with ten real jobs from your work, run them all, and get total cost and average score per model. That's no longer a one-off test, it's a small evaluation, and it works to defend a decision in a meeting

Add an automatic judge: a model scores the others' answers with your same rubric. Compare its score with yours on the ten tasks and measure how closely they match. If they agree, you can automate the boring part; if not, now you know not to trust a model judging models
defend: Question: 'Where do you store the keys, and what do you do if one leaks?'. Answer: outside the code, in a .env file the program reads at startup and that's in .gitignore, so it never leaves the computer. The code only knows the variable's name, never the value. And if a key leaks, you don't touch the code: you go into the provider's dashboard, revoke that key, and generate a new one. Revoking is instant and irreversible, which is exactly what you need when someone has your key and is spending your balance.

Question: 'How do you know the cost you calculate is the real one?'. Answer: I don't estimate the tokens, I read them from the usage field each API returns in its own response, which is the same count they bill you with. Prices are in a separate data file, with the date I checked them, because they change every few months. And there's a detail a lot of people miss: in reasoning models, thinking tokens get billed as output and arrive in a separate field, so if you don't add them in, the cost comes out short.

Question: 'Your table says the cheap model wins. Would you put it into production tomorrow?'. Answer: not with this test. This is a comparison, not an evaluation: one prompt, one run, and a score I set myself. It's good for ruling things out and pointing a direction, not for closing the decision. For production you'd need to repeat each case several times for variability, have twenty or thirty representative examples, a right-or-wrong criterion written before reading the answers, and also measure failures: how many times you have to retry, because a retry gets billed twice.
